opts.t: Anterior cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves
opts.why: Anterior intercostal branches provide medial/anterior breast sensation and are not the exception.
Supraclavicular sensory nerves contribute to upper breast skin sensation.

opts.t: Lateral cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves
opts.why: Lateral intercostal cutaneous branches supply lateral breast and axillary extension.

questions.expl: Breast skin receives anterior and lateral thoracic intercostal branches and superior supraclavicular contributions. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi (motor), not breast cutaneous sensation.

questions.stem: The recommended antibiotic prophylaxis for surgical termination of pregnancy is

opts.why: Cefazolin is general surgical prophylaxis, not the specified doxycycline regimen for surgical termination.
Cephalexin is not the recalled recommended prophylaxis regimen and has different STI coverage.
Clindamycin IV is an alternative in selected circumstances, not the standard oral doxycycline regimen.

questions.expl: Antibiotic prophylaxis for surgical abortion reduces post-procedure infection. A doxycycline 400 mg oral regimen is one accepted Australian regimen; actual timing and choice follow local guidance.
questions.note: Historical recalled dose; contemporary protocols may use split-dose doxycycline.

questions.stem: The water capacity of an oxygen transport cylinder is 2 litres. The gauge is reading 150 bar. At an oxygen flow rate of 10 litres per minute, the number of minutes the cylinder will last is

opts.why: 60 minutes would need 600 L, twice the 300 L cylinder gas estimate.
15 minutes uses only half of the available 300 L at 10 L/min.
45 minutes would require 450 L, exceeding 2×150 L.

questions.expl: Available gas ≈ water capacity × pressure = 2 L × 150 bar = 300 L; at 10 L/min this lasts 30 minutes, assuming full use of the cylinder contents.

questions.stem: Risk factors for chronic post-surgical pain do NOT include

opts.why: Younger age is a recognised predictor of persistent postsurgical pain.
Pre-existing chronic pain is a strong predictor of later postsurgical pain.
Anxiety/catastrophising can increase pain persistence through psychosocial vulnerability.

questions.expl: Poorer psychosocial circumstances and previous pain increase persistent postsurgical pain risk. Higher education is not a typical risk factor in the recalled choice set.
questions.note: Risk associations vary by operation and population; this is a recalled-option comparison.

questions.stem: The anion which contributes the most to the anion gap is

opts.why: Phosphate contributes an unmeasured anion but normally less than albumin.
Bicarbonate is a measured anion explicitly subtracted in the anion-gap formula.
Chloride is another measured subtracted anion rather than the principal unmeasured component.

questions.expl: Albumin is the principal unmeasured anion contributing to the conventional anion gap. Chloride and bicarbonate are measured ions subtracted in the calculation.

questions.stem: You are resuscitating a 60 kg man in cardiac arrest secondary to severe hyperkalaemia. You decide to give intravenous sodium bicarbonate. Australian and New Zealand resuscitation guidelines state the initial dose of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate should be

opts.why: 100 mL gives 100 mmol, above 60 mmol in the exam-era 1-mmol/kg dose.
20 mL gives only 20 mmol, one-third the calculated patient dose.
10 mL is a sixth of the 60-mL dose derived from 1 mL/kg.

questions.expl: The exam-era dose was 1 mmol/kg (1 mL/kg of 8.4%) for hyperkalaemic arrest, so a 60 kg patient receives 60 mL. Modern ANZCOR guidance may use a different fixed adult dose; this is historical exam dosing.
questions.note: Historical answer differs from newer ANZCOR 2026 hyperkalaemia guidance.

questions.stem: Prothrombinex VF is a factor concentrate. It is indicated for the management of bleeding caused by

opts.why: Factor VIII replacement is required for haemophilia A; Prothrombinex is not FVIII concentrate.
Congenital fibrinogen deficiency calls for fibrinogen-containing replacement, not PCC.
VWD usually needs VWF-containing concentrate or adjunctive therapy, not factor IX PCC.

questions.expl: Prothrombinex VF contains vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors including factor IX and was used as a factor IX-containing concentrate. It is not a factor VIII, VWF or fibrinogen replacement product.
questions.note: Historical product formulations and indications vary by country/time; consult current product data for clinical use.

questions.stem: A patient has a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) inserted. The follow-up chest X-ray shows the tip positioned in the (Chest X-Ray shown)

opts.why: A true lower SVC tip should align along the central caval contour, rather than curl into azygos arch.
Right atrial placement is distal to the cavoatrial junction and not the recalled radiographic position.
Cavoatrial junction lies inferior to azygos arch entry; the tip course was recalled as azygos malposition.

questions.expl: The recalled question-bank key identified malposition into the azygos vein. A catheter directed posteriorly into the azygos arch can be mistaken for a central SVC tip. The original radiograph is not published.
questions.note: The practice image is illustrative; without the original chest radiograph the ANZCA image diagnosis cannot be authenticated.

questions.stem: You are called to assist with a patient in the intensive care unit who has had cardiac surgery three days ago and is now in cardiac arrest. External cardiac massage should aim for a systolic blood pressure of

opts.why: 80 mmHg exceeds the cited post-cardiac-surgery compression systolic target.
120 mmHg is not the target minimum during chest compressions after sternotomy.
40 mmHg falls below the target and may indicate inadequate compressions.

questions.expl: After cardiac surgery, arterial pressure during external chest compressions should yield systolic impulses >60 mmHg while preparations for emergency resternotomy proceed.

questions.stem: You have been asked to anaesthetise a patient with a history of severe depression that has been well controlled on moclobemide. The most appropriate medications in combination with propofol are

opts.why: Pethidine is serotonergic and can precipitate serious interaction with moclobemide.
Ephedrine indirectly releases catecholamines and is inappropriate in MAO-inhibited patients.
Ephedrine remains problematic; fentanyl can have serotonergic interaction potential.

questions.expl: Avoid pethidine/tramadol and caution with serotonergic opioids or indirectly acting sympathomimetics when using MAO inhibitors. Phenylephrine is direct acting; sevoflurane and morphine are suitable.
questions.note: Moclobemide is a reversible MAO-A inhibitor; interactions and patient-specific continuation plans require review.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient who has undergone trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy for a growth-hormone secreting adenoma has a urine output of one litre in the first postoperative hour. The following results are obtained. The most appropriate early management is (Urine and serum biochemistry shown)

opts.why: Hypertonic saline worsens hypernatraemia and does not replace missing AVP.

opts.t: No intervention until the next day
opts.why: Large water losses can rapidly raise sodium; leaving untreated for a day is unsafe.
Fluid restriction worsens dehydration/hypernatraemia during diabetes insipidus.

questions.expl: Abrupt polyuria with high plasma osmolality and inadequately dilute urine after pituitary surgery suggests central diabetes insipidus. Desmopressin with close sodium and fluid-balance monitoring addresses AVP deficiency.
questions.note: Recalled figures: sodium ~145, serum osmolality ~320, urine osmolality ~200 mOsm/kg. These are not reproduced in the ANZCA report; if haemodynamically unstable, resuscitate intravascular volume first.
questions.imgcap: Reconstructed practice image/table; the 2020.2 Chair’s Report does not reproduce this diagnostic figure or data.

questions.stem: The main advantage of using noradrenaline over phenylephrine for the prevention of hypotension as a result spinal anaesthesia for elective Casearean Section is

opts.t: Less maternal bradycardia and better cardiac-output preservation

opts.why: Noradrenaline's half-life is short and longer persistence is not the demonstrated advantage.

opts.t: Better fetal acid-base outcomes proven in all cases
opts.why: An across-the-board neonatal acid–base improvement over phenylephrine has not been proven.
Pure phenylephrine is associated with more bradycardia; noradrenaline does not characteristically increase it.

questions.expl: Norepinephrine has some β1 activity, preserving heart rate and cardiac output compared with pure α agonist phenylephrine. A consistent fetal outcome benefit has not been established.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man suffers a hydrofluoric acid burn to 60% of his total body surface area in an industrial accident. An expected electrolyte disturbance is

opts.why: Phosphate may change in severe injury but is not the defining fluoride-chelation abnormality.
Hypernatraemia is not a direct expected consequence of hydrofluoric acid.
Fluoride complexes calcium, decreasing rather than increasing its free serum level.

questions.expl: Fluoride ions avidly bind calcium and magnesium after hydrofluoric acid exposure, causing severe hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia with dysrhythmia risk.

questions.stem: An ASA 1 28 year old male attends for inguinal hernia repair under general anaesthesia. He is administered propofol 180mg morphine 8mg rocuronium 50mg cephazolin 2g Post induction he develops an erythematous rash on his chest and arms, swelling of his lips and face, and severe hypotension. Preliminary blood results show … The most likely diagnosis is (biochemical blood tests relevant to allergy shown)

opts.why: Malignant hyperthermia is mainly hypermetabolic and does not characteristically cause immediate urticaria/angioedema.

opts.t: Isolated opioid histamine release without systemic compromise
opts.why: Opioid histamine release alone rarely explains the severe shock plus mucosal oedema described.
No local anaesthetic was administered; LAST cannot explain this post-induction syndrome.

questions.expl: Rapid mucocutaneous features, angioedema and cardiovascular collapse after induction strongly support perioperative anaphylaxis. Rocuronium/cefazolin are plausible triggers, but specific culprit requires formal testing.
questions.note: Original tryptase values omitted; clinical anaphylaxis can be recognised without a positive assay; do not assert a proven culprit from the stem alone.

questions.stem: A patient with a purely metabolic acidosis has a serum bicarbonate of 14 mmol/L and a lactate of 3.8 mmol/L. The expected PaCO2 is

opts.why: 40 mmHg is above Winter's predicted 29 mmHg and would indicate additional respiratory acidosis.
50 mmHg is markedly too high, suggesting major concomitant ventilatory failure.
20 mmHg is below the expected range and suggests a second respiratory alkalosis.

questions.expl: Winter's formula: expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃ + 8 ± 2 = 1.5 ×14 + 8 = 29 ±2 mmHg. Outside this range, consider an additional respiratory disorder.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis has had a recent transthoracic echocardiogram to evaluate pulmonary pressure and suitability for lung transplantation. Below is a continuous wave Doppler trace through the tricuspid valve. Her central venous pressure is 5 mmHg. Her estimated right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) is (Echocardiography doppler trace shown)

opts.why: 65 mmHg requires a higher TR jet velocity than the illustrative 3 m/s.
55 mmHg similarly overestimates 4×3²+5.
29 mmHg underestimates the jet-derived 36-mmHg gradient even before RAP is added.

questions.expl: RVSP ≈ 4 × (peak TR velocity)² + RAP. If an illustrative trace shows 3.0 m/s with RAP 5 mmHg, RVSP = 36 + 5 = 41 mmHg.
questions.note: The official report omits the TR Doppler velocity. Synthetic 3.0 m/s trace is for calculation practice, NOT the original numerical answer.

questions.stem: In maternal cardiac arrest the most common arrhythmia is

opts.why: Monomorphic VT is a less frequent initial maternal arrest rhythm than PEA.
Torsades is uncommon as the presenting obstetric arrest rhythm.
VF is possible but not the leading initial maternal arrest rhythm in the cited data.

questions.expl: Maternal arrest is frequently due to haemorrhage, hypoxia or embolic processes and commonly presents as PEA rather than a shockable rhythm.

questions.stem: The initial dose of IV adrenaline recommended for Grade 2 (moderate) anaphylaxis in an adult is

opts.why: 500 µg is a typical adult IM dose in community anaphylaxis, not a titrated IV grade-2 bolus.
5 mg IV is massively excessive outside any routine anaphylaxis bolus algorithm.
1 mg IV is an adult cardiac-arrest dose, much too large for moderate perioperative anaphylaxis.

questions.expl: In an appropriately monitored perioperative setting, a 10–20 microgram IV bolus is used in some grade-2 anaphylaxis algorithms for an anaesthetist able to titrate it. IM 500 micrograms remains standard first-line in most community settings.
questions.note: Clinical grades and IV doses vary across guidelines; use local perioperative anaphylaxis algorithm.

questions.stem: You are conducting a departmental audit and after 100 patients you have zero cases of dental damage. Your director asks you if you can estimate the risk of dental damage. You tell them that the approximate upper 95% confidence interval for the risk would be

opts.why: 10% overestimates the upper 95% risk boundary for zero events in 100.
30% is ten times the 3%-rule upper bound.
0.3% is too narrow; with zero observed events, a 3% risk remains plausible.

questions.expl: Rule of three: with zero events in 100 independent observations, the approximate upper 95% confidence boundary is 3/100 = 3%.

questions.stem: Complications of hyperbaric oxygen therapy do NOT include

opts.why: Oxygen-induced seizures are a recognised CNS oxygen-toxicity complication of HBOT.
Transient myopia is a known repeated-exposure effect.
Barotrauma from chamber pressure changes commonly affects the middle ear.

questions.expl: HBOT is associated with pressure injury, oxygen-toxicity seizures and myopic changes. Central retinal artery occlusion is an indication considered for HBOT, not a recognised usual adverse effect.

questions.stem: You are anaesthetising a 35 year old woman undergoing a laparoscopic appendicectomy. She uses a levonorgestrel-secreting intrauterine device (MirenaTM) for contraception and you have used sugammadex for reversal of neuromuscular blockade at the end of the procedure. Your post-operative advice to her regarding contraception should state that

opts.t: No changes necessary because Mirena is unaffected
opts.why: Levonorgestrel exposure may be affected; Mirena users need the same seven-day barrier advice after sugammadex.
Removing the IUD is unnecessary and would compromise ongoing contraception.
Twenty-four hours is shorter than the product's backup-contraception period.

questions.expl: Sugammadex may decrease exposure to progestogens; non-oral hormonal contraceptive users are advised barrier contraception for 7 days afterward.

questions.stem: In cardiac surgery, volatile-based anaesthesia compared to total intravenous anaesthesia

opts.t: No significant difference in 1-year mortality in a large randomized CABG trial
Volatiles abolish the risk of postoperative renal injury
opts.why: Renal injury can still occur after CABG with volatile or intravenous anaesthesia.
MYRIAD did not demonstrate a halving of one-year mortality with volatiles.
TIVA did not double postoperative MI compared with volatile anaesthesia.

questions.expl: MYRIAD (2019) found no significant 1-year survival advantage with volatile versus intravenous anaesthesia in elective CABG. Earlier meta-analyses suggested possible benefit, creating a historical recall discrepancy.
questions.note: The original five-option choice set is unavailable; evidence-based answer reflects MYRIAD rather than an older positive meta-analysis.

questions.stem: Interventions that reduce the risk of agitation following electroconvulsive therapy include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: A quiet recovery setting can reduce sensory overload and postoperative agitation.
Dexmedetomidine may reduce emergence agitation when appropriate.

opts.t: Treating established agitation with carefully titrated benzodiazepine
opts.why: Judicious benzodiazepines can treat significant agitation after assessment.

opts.t: Using ketamine as the sole anaesthetic expressly to prevent emergence agitation

questions.expl: Quiet recovery, dexmedetomidine and judicious benzodiazepines can reduce post-ECT agitation or treat it. Ketamine can increase emergence phenomena and is not a reliable agitation-prevention strategy.
questions.note: The ANZCA report omits original options; reconstructed EXCEPT item is not an authenticated recollection.

opts.why: Pleural fluid lies outside stomach and has a different sonographic location.
Clear liquid distends the gastric antrum rather than producing a collapsed target appearance.
Solid content is echogenic/heterogeneous rather than an empty flat 'bull's eye'.

questions.expl: An empty antrum has a flat or collapsed 'bull's eye' appearance. Clear fluid distends the lumen, and solid contents create heterogeneous echoes.

questions.stem: Intraoperative cell salvage is contraindicated in

opts.t: Patient refusal of allogeneic blood but acceptance of salvage
opts.why: Patients declining donor blood may specifically accept a closed-circuit salvage technique.

opts.t: Contamination with substances capable of red-cell lysis (e.g. hydrogen peroxide)

opts.why: Obstetric salvage is possible with appropriate washing, leukocyte filtration and patient discussion.
Major vascular surgery is a common indication for cell salvage, not a contraindication.

questions.expl: Cell salvage returns washed RBCs and can be appropriate in major vascular and obstetric surgery; certain haemolytic chemicals in the field make salvaged blood unsafe.
questions.note: Infected/contaminated fields are relative rather than universally absolute contraindications; patient wishes remain decisive.

questions.stem: The most likely diagnosis in a 45-year-old man with the above biochemistry is (liver function tests shown)

opts.why: Haemolysis typically produces indirect bilirubin without the mixed inflammatory biliary context.
Alcoholic hepatitis usually gives AST-predominant hepatocellular abnormalities and relevant exposure history.
Acute viral hepatitis often gives much higher ALT/AST than mild cholestatic changes.

questions.expl: The recalled bank identified cholecystitis. Mild cholestatic biochemistry may accompany gallbladder disease, but LFTs alone cannot establish cholecystitis without clinical features and imaging.

questions.stem: Piped oxygen supply in major hospitals is predominantly sourced from

opts.why: Nitrous oxide is a different medical gas and not the hospital's bulk oxygen source.

opts.t: Oxygen concentrators in every operating theatre
opts.why: Individual concentrators may exist but do not generally supply every theatre in a major hospital.
Small cylinders are backup/transport rather than the predominant bulk piped source.

questions.expl: Large hospitals generally receive and store cryogenic liquid oxygen in a vacuum-insulated evaporator (VIE), feeding a piped oxygen distribution system.

questions.stem: Application of a pacemaker magnet to a ventricular implanted pacemaker would be expected to convert the operating mode to

opts.why: VVI is inhibited on sensed ventricular beats and is not the usual default magnet asynchronous mode.
AAI paces/senses atrium and is not the ventricular magnet mode.
DDD tracks both chambers and remains sensing-dependent, unlike asynchronous VOO.

questions.expl: A magnet generally drives conventional ventricular pacemakers to a manufacturer-specific asynchronous mode; VOO means ventricular paced, none sensed, no sensing response.
questions.note: Magnet response depends on device, battery status and manufacturer; some devices are programmable.

questions.stem: The optimal position, under ultrasound guidance, to place a catheter tip to provide continuous erector spinae plane block for post-thoracotomy analgesia is

opts.t: Superficial to the erector spinae fascia
opts.why: Superficial fascial injection misses the deep erector-spinae/transverse-process interface.
Intramuscular injection may remain localised and does not reliably spread in the interfascial plane.

opts.t: Inside the paravertebral space beneath pleura
opts.why: Paravertebral placement is deeper and a different block target, potentially with greater procedural risk.

opts.t: In the plane deep to erector spinae and superficial to a transverse process

questions.expl: The ESP block targets the fascial plane between erector spinae and transverse processes to promote longitudinal local-anaesthetic spread.

questions.stem: The maximum warm ischaemic time (in minutes) acceptable for procuring the lungs following donation after cardiac death is

opts.why: Thirty minutes is shorter than the period-specific recalled lung DCD threshold.
240 minutes exceeds the common upper warm-ischaemia allowance for lung procurement.
Fifteen minutes is much shorter than the recalled acceptable limit.

questions.expl: A commonly taught DCD-lung acceptable warm-ischaemia period is approximately 90 minutes, although transplant protocols define different start and end points and may be more restrictive.
questions.note: Depends on DCD type and whether functional warm ischaemia is measured; this is period-specific recall.

questions.stem: A 25 year old ASA 1 patient develops ongoing seizures 5 minutes after receiving a brachial plexus block with ropivacaine. Of the following, the most suitable initial intravenous treatment is

opts.why: Giving more ropivacaine worsens local anaesthetic systemic toxicity and seizures.
Physostigmine treats selected anticholinergic toxicity, not sodium-channel-mediated LAST seizures.
Dantrolene is used for MH, not initial control of LAST seizures.

opts.t: Midazolam IV to terminate seizures, with LAST resuscitation prepared

questions.expl: Benzodiazepines treat LAST-associated seizures while airway/oxygenation and lipid-emulsion therapy are prepared. Cardiac instability calls for immediate lipid therapy and adapted resuscitation.
questions.note: Dose and sequence must follow current ASRA/ANZCA LAST algorithm.

questions.stem: Hepcidin production is inhibited in response to

opts.why: High iron stores increase hepcidin as feedback against further iron uptake.
Inflammatory IL-6 induces hepcidin and reduces iron availability.
Infection-associated inflammation tends to raise, not suppress, hepcidin.

questions.expl: Low oxygen delivery, anaemia and enhanced erythropoiesis suppress hepcidin to increase intestinal iron absorption and iron release. IL-6 and iron loading increase hepcidin.

questions.stem: Compared to a normothermic patient, a patient with mild intraoperative hypothermia (35.0 oC) will have

opts.why: Hypothermia impairs haemostasis and generally increases, not reduces, blood loss.
Platelet function deteriorates, so bleeding time would not be reliably shortened.

opts.t: Increased blood loss despite potentially normal routine clotting times

opts.why: Normal platelet function cannot be assumed when core temperature falls to 35°C.

questions.expl: Mild hypothermia impairs platelet and coagulation-enzyme function and increases bleeding. Laboratory assays performed at 37°C may conceal in-vivo temperature-dependent changes.

questions.stem: Following a severe spinal cord injury, return of reflexes is usually seen after

opts.why: Spinal shock typically lasts longer than ten minutes before reflexes reappear.

opts.t: Never after complete spinal cord injury
opts.why: Spinal cord injury can initially suppress but does not permanently abolish all segmental reflexes.
Some reflexes return over days, well before 6–12 months in many cases.

questions.expl: During spinal shock there is initial areflexia; some segmental reflexes typically begin to return over days, whereas brisk hyperreflexia and spasticity evolve over weeks to months.

questions.stem: Abuse of nitrous oxide may lead to

opts.t: Functional vitamin B12 inactivation causing myeloneuropathy

opts.why: N₂O oxidises and inactivates B12 rather than causing excess vitamin B12 activity.
Vitamin D production is not the mechanism of N₂O-related neuropathy.
Methionine synthase is inhibited, not chronically stimulated, by N₂O exposure.

questions.expl: Nitrous oxide oxidises the cobalt moiety of vitamin B12, inhibiting methionine synthase and causing subacute combined degeneration or neuropathy with repeated exposure.

questions.stem: When using 'Level 1 Fast Flow Fluid Warmer' rapid fluid infuser system, of the following the device that delivers the greatest flow is a (list of intravascular cannulae)

opts.why: 20-gauge tubing has relatively high resistance and lower rapid-infusion flow.
Long narrow central lumens are flow-limited despite central placement.
A 22-gauge long catheter offers even higher resistance than short large-bore access.

questions.expl: For rapid pressure-assisted infusion, short wide cannulae deliver substantially greater flow than long narrow catheters (Poiseuille relation).
questions.note: Original offered cannula dimensions were omitted; this is a representative option set.

questions.stem: The changes in oximetry seen after intravenous injection of indocyanine green are

opts.t: Permanent severe reduction in true SaO₂
opts.why: Indocyanine green changes optical absorption, not actual SaO₂ permanently.
Transient pulse-ox/NIRS artefacts can be seen after ICG injection.

opts.t: Increase in SpO₂ and decrease in NIRS in every patient
opts.why: SpO₂ usually falls transiently rather than universally rising with NIRS falling.

opts.t: Decrease in pulse-oximeter SpO₂ with transient interference/elevation in some cerebral NIRS readings

questions.expl: Indocyanine green absorbs near-infrared light and may transiently perturb optical saturation devices without changing true arterial oxygenation. Direction of NIRS bias is device-dependent.
questions.note: The recorded effect depends on wavelength and monitor; do not infer genuine desaturation from dye artefact.

questions.stem: A patient has prolonged surgery with a laryngeal mask airway. The following day she reports a problem with her tongue. You examine her and see the following when she protrudes her tongue. The most likely cause of the abnormality is (picture of a person’s face shown)

opts.why: Glossopharyngeal nerve mediates posterior tongue sensation/swallowing, not genioglossus movement.
Recurrent laryngeal affects vocal cords/voice, not protrusion toward the affected side.
Facial nerve controls facial expression, not motor innervation of tongue.

questions.expl: Unilateral deviation of the protruded tongue toward the weak side indicates ipsilateral hypoglossal (XII) dysfunction, reported with airway-device compression.

questions.stem: The therapy most likely to decrease mortality in neonates with congenital diaphragmatic hernia is

opts.t: Universal emergent ECMO for every neonate
opts.why: ECMO is a rescue in selected infants, not universally indicated for every CDH case.
Aggressive hyperventilation and alkalosis can cause barotrauma and worsen pulmonary damage.
High-pressure bag ventilation damages hypoplastic lungs and increases pulmonary hypertension.

opts.t: Gentle lung-protective ventilation and avoidance of barotrauma

questions.expl: In congenital diaphragmatic hernia, low-pressure 'gentle' ventilation reduces ventilator-induced injury; routine aggressive ventilation worsens pulmonary damage.
questions.note: Multiple concurrent improvements affect CDH outcomes; no single isolated mortality benefit universally applies.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man suffers a 30% total body surface area burn. A cardiovascular physiological change expected within the first 24 hours is

opts.t: Reduced vascular resistance from vasodilation immediately
opts.why: Initial burns cause vasoconstriction and increased rather than reduced systemic resistance.

opts.t: Increased cardiac output during first hours
opts.why: Cardiac output often initially falls due to capillary leak and reduced preload.
Ventricular filling is compromised without replacement of intravascular losses.

opts.t: Increased systemic and pulmonary vascular resistance early after major burns

questions.expl: Early burn shock produces catecholamine-mediated vasoconstriction, capillary leak, hypovolaemia and decreased cardiac output; high-output physiology evolves later.

questions.stem: Methylene blue may be used in the treatment of all of the following conditions EXCEPT

opts.why: Methylene blue is used as rescue for some vasoplegia by inhibiting NO–guanylate cyclase signalling.
Selected ifosfamide encephalopathy can respond to methylene blue.

opts.t: Treatment of toxicity in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

opts.why: It is the classic antidote for acquired methemoglobinaemia in patients without G6PD deficiency.

questions.expl: Methylene blue is used for methemoglobinaemia and refractory vasoplegia, but is ineffective/dangerous in G6PD deficiency because NADPH generation is impaired and haemolysis can follow.

questions.stem: The substance that should be avoided in a patient with history of anaphylaxis to MMR vaccine is

opts.why: Balanced crystalloid does not contain gelatin antigen and is ordinarily acceptable.
Human albumin is not gelatin-based and does not share the suspected vaccine antigen.
Normal saline is not gelatin-derived and has no expected gelatin cross-reactivity.

questions.expl: Some severe MMR vaccine reactions reflect gelatin allergy, so gelatin-derived colloid should be avoided pending allergy assessment. MMR allergy alone does not establish gelatin sensitisation in every case.
questions.note: Check the documented cause of the vaccine reaction; gelatin is not the only potential trigger.

Right thoracotomy without abdominal phase misses the stomach mobilization needed in open Ivor–Lewis.
A left thoracotomy is not the standard right-sided Ivor–Lewis thoracic access.

questions.expl: Open Ivor-Lewis oesophagectomy uses an abdominal phase to mobilise stomach and a right thoracic phase for resection/intrathoracic anastomosis.

150 cmH₂O is even further above safe LMA cuff pressure.
20 cmH₂O may be used as a low cuff pressure but is not the stated upper limit of 60.

questions.stem: International guidelines state that patients presenting for major surgery have inadequate or low iron stores if their serum ferritin level is less than

opts.t: Ferritin below 300 only in every patient
opts.why: 300 µg/L is not the absolute deficiency threshold; high ferritin needs inflammatory interpretation.
1000 µg/L is far above ferritin concentrations used to diagnose absolute deficiency.
500 µg/L alone does not establish depleted iron stores.

questions.expl: Ferritin <30 µg/L indicates absolute iron deficiency in non-inflammatory states. In inflammation, a ferritin up to 100 with low TSAT may still indicate iron deficiency.

questions.stem: You are part of an international humanitarian aid mission. You have packed sevoflurane but the only local vaporiser is isoflurane specific with a maximum output of 5%. If you added sevoflurane to the isoflurane vaporiser the maximum sevoflurane output percentage would be approximately (Sevoflurane saturated vapour pressure 160mmHg, isoflurane 240mmHg)

opts.why: 1% ignores the vapour-pressure ratio and underestimates sevo output.
5% assumes identical saturated vapour pressure for iso and sevo.
7.5% would imply sevo had higher saturated vapour pressure than iso, opposite to the given ratio.

questions.expl: A vapouriser calibrated to isoflurane will deliver approximately 5% × (sevo saturated vapour pressure 160 / isoflurane 240) = 3.33% sevoflurane at maximum dial setting.
questions.note: Cross-filling vaporizers is unsafe; a calculation exercise only.

questions.stem: A Jehovah’s Witness patient attends for a revision total hip replacement and is medically optimized. You consider she is high risk for the procedure but after extensive discussion agree to proceed, including agreeing that you will not give blood under any circumstances. Your decision can be justified on the basis of

opts.t: Obligation to transfuse against valid refusal
opts.why: A valid informed refusal must not be overridden solely on clinician preference.
Paternalism disregards the competent patient's expressed values.
Withholding material risk information undermines informed refusal and shared decision-making.

questions.expl: An informed adult's refusal of blood products should be respected even when medically risky. Decision-making requires disclosure, capacity and documentation.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male, three days post laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy has ongoing nausea and vomiting. His arterial blood gas measurement is as follows: (ABG shown) The best initial therapeutic option would be

opts.why: Dialysis is not first-line for chloride-depletion alkalosis due to postoperative emesis.

opts.t: IV isotonic saline and potassium replacement if indicated (reconstructed alkalosis)

opts.why: Sodium bicarbonate worsens metabolic alkalosis rather than correcting it.
Hypertonic saline is not routinely indicated for vomiting-induced hypochloraemic alkalosis.

questions.expl: Protracted emesis after bariatric surgery often produces chloride-depletion metabolic alkalosis with hypochloraemia/hypokalaemia, for which isotonic saline and chloride/potassium replacement are appropriate.
questions.note: Original ABG omitted. The recalled key favours saline/potassium; reconstructed values, not ANZCA data, are used for practice.

questions.stem: The nerve(s) that need to be blocked with local anaesthetic to achieve complete anaesthesia for amputation of the fifth toe is/are

opts.why: Common fibular alone misses the plantar aspect supplied by tibial nerve.
Femoral nerve does not innervate fifth-toe plantar/dorsolateral digital surfaces.
Saphenous supplies medial foot rather than the lateral fifth toe.

questions.expl: The fifth toe receives plantar digital sensory branches from tibial nerve and dorsal contributions from superficial fibular nerve, so both distributions need local anaesthetic coverage.

questions.stem: A patient has numbness and weakness in her hand post operatively. You are trying to distinguish between an ulnar nerve lesion and a C8 / T1 radiculopathy. You can diagnose a C8 / T1 radiculopathy if she has weakness

opts.why: Interossei are ulnar-innervated and can be weak in isolated ulnar neuropathy.
Adductor pollicis is ulnar motor and does not distinguish a root from an ulnar nerve lesion.

opts.t: Sensory loss over the little finger alone
opts.why: Little-finger sensory loss is classic ulnar distribution, not evidence of a second median/C8-T1 muscle deficit.

questions.expl: C8/T1 radiculopathy can impair median-innervated thenar muscles, unlike an isolated ulnar lesion. Abductor pollicis brevis is median-innervated and tests a non-ulnar C8/T1 muscle.

questions.stem: You are asked to review a patient who underwent upper limb surgery. During the procedure the anaesthetist placed a nerve block. The patient has weakness on external shoulder rotation and atrophy of supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. The nerve most likely to have been injured is the

opts.why: Axillary nerve primarily innervates deltoid and teres minor, not both supra- and infraspinatus.
Long thoracic controls serratus anterior and scapular winging, not rotator-cuff external rotation.
Musculocutaneous controls biceps/brachialis and forearm flexion, not the described rotator cuff muscles.

questions.expl: The suprascapular nerve innervates supraspinatus and infraspinatus; injury weakens initiation of abduction and external shoulder rotation with wasting of both muscles.

questions.stem: The muscle or muscle group with the greatest sensitivity to the action of non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agents is the

opts.why: The diaphragm is relatively resistant to nondepolarising blockade.
Laryngeal adductors are relatively resistant compared with adductor pollicis.
Corrugator supercilii often tracks laryngeal onset and is less sensitive than adductor pollicis.

opts.t: Adductor pollicis (among the listed comparator muscles)

questions.expl: Adductor pollicis is more sensitive to nondepolarising blockade than diaphragm and laryngeal adductors, making it a useful surrogate for residual weakness. Upper-airway/pharyngeal sensitivity can vary by muscle.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and chronic obstructive airway disease, treated with digoxin 125mcg, salbutamol and salmeterol, develops a wheeze intraoperatively which responds to salbutamol via the endotracheal tube. The patient then develops rapid atrial fibrillation with a rate of 120 bpm, a BP of 90/60 and an ETCO2 of 40mmHg. The next most suitable treatment option is

opts.t: Carefully titrated IV amiodarone, with rhythm and haemodynamic reassessment
Routine high-dose IV beta blocker during active bronchospasm
opts.why: Large beta-blocker boluses may worsen bronchospasm and hypotension in borderline AF.
Salbutamol can provoke tachycardia and is not ventricular-rate control for AF.

opts.t: Unsynchronised cardioversion in a perfusing stable rhythm
opts.why: Unsynchronised cardioversion is not the response to a perfusing rhythm; unstable AF requires synchronised shock.

questions.expl: Rapid AF with marginal pressure and recent bronchospasm calls for assessment of instability, correction of triggers and a drug that avoids aggravating bronchospasm. Amiodarone is a possible recalled choice; unstable AF requires synchronised cardioversion.
questions.note: Anki and Brainscape disagree on preferred antiarrhythmic; no original options, so this is a reconstructed decision rather than the official key.

questions.stem: CYP2D6 variability has NO effect on the metabolism of

opts.why: Codeine requires CYP2D6 conversion to morphine for much of its activity.
Hydrocodone metabolism includes CYP2D6 production of hydromorphone.
Tramadol requires CYP2D6 to generate its potent M1 opioid metabolite.

questions.expl: Hydromorphone undergoes mainly glucuronidation, unlike codeine, tramadol and hydrocodone whose activation/metabolism is influenced by CYP2D6 genotype.

questions.stem: The minimum macroshock current required to elicit ventricular fibrillation is

opts.why: One microampere is far below the approximate external macroshock VF threshold.
100 µA pertains to direct intracardiac microshock, not current traversing intact chest.
Ten amperes greatly exceeds macroshock VF induction levels and would cause severe injury.

questions.expl: Macroshock across the chest generally requires current on the order of 100 mA to induce VF, versus ≈100 µA applied directly to the myocardium (microshock).

questions.stem: A patient undergoing robotic prostatectomy, with controlled mandatory volume ventilation, has the following measurements: plateau pressure 32 cmH2O, PEEP 8 cmH2O, autoPEEP 4 cmH2O, peak pressure 38 cmH2O, tidal volume 600mL The static compliance is

opts.why: 40 would require only a 15-cmH₂O driving pressure; actual driving pressure is 20.
25 miscalculates the effective pressure denominator of 32−12.
20 reflects an excessive assumed driving pressure and does not equal 600/20.

questions.expl: Static compliance = tidal volume / (plateau pressure − total PEEP) = 600 / (32 − (8+4)) = 30 mL/cmH₂O.

questions.stem: In the POISE study the use of beta blockers on the day of surgery as a cardio protective strategy in high risk patients has been associated with

opts.why: POISE-1 found more deaths/strokes despite fewer MIs, not a net survival benefit.

opts.t: Reduced stroke with increased myocardial infarction
opts.why: Stroke increased, while nonfatal MI decreased—not the reverse.
There were measurable benefits and harms; the result was not null.

opts.t: Increased all-cause mortality and stroke despite fewer nonfatal myocardial infarctions

questions.expl: POISE-1 showed perioperative high-dose metoprolol reduced nonfatal MI but increased stroke and mortality, cautioning against acute blanket β-blockade.

questions.stem: The currently recommended antiseptic solution for skin preparation use before neuraxial blockade is

opts.why: Povidone/peroxide mixtures are not the recommended validated neuraxial skin preparation.
Soap without antiseptic action is insufficient infection prevention at neuraxial puncture.

opts.t: Alcoholic chlorhexidine preparation suitable for neuraxial procedures

opts.why: Unsterile water alone does not provide validated procedural antisepsis.

questions.expl: ANZCA infection-control guidance recommends alcoholic chlorhexidine skin preparation using an appropriate formulation and allowing it to dry fully before needle insertion.
questions.note: Historical concentration often quoted 0.5%; follow current local chlorhexidine safety policy.

questions.stem: Elimination of remifentanil occurs following breakdown mainly by

opts.t: Renal filtration of intact drug only
opts.why: Remifentanil does not rely primarily on unchanged renal filtration to terminate effect.
Plasma pseudocholinesterase is not its exclusive metabolic route; tissue esterases dominate.
Hepatic CYP2D6 activity does not determine remifentanil's rapid hydrolysis.

questions.expl: Remifentanil is hydrolysed rapidly by nonspecific tissue and blood esterases, accounting for its context-insensitive rapid offset.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has a right heart catheter for investigation of recent onset dyspnoea below. Her pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 10mmHg. The most likely diagnosis is

opts.t: Precapillary pulmonary hypertension, potentially due to pulmonary embolic disease

opts.why: Pulmonary arterial hypertension with elevated PVR is not normal pulmonary haemodynamics.

opts.t: Isolated left-heart failure with elevated wedge pressure
opts.why: An isolated left-heart cause usually has PCWP above 15 mmHg rather than 10.

opts.t: Constrictive pericarditis proven from wedge alone
opts.why: Wedge pressure alone cannot prove constrictive pericarditis, which needs additional haemodynamic features.

opts.why: Pulse oximetry is essential continuous monitoring of oxygenation in GA.
Oxygen analyser measures delivered inspired oxygen and is a fundamental required safety monitor.
Capnography is required for ventilation confirmation under intubated/paralysed GA.

questions.stem: Of the following, the agent that causes the LEAST prolongation of the Thrombin Clotting Time (or Thrombin Time) is

opts.why: Heparin directly potentiates antithrombin inhibition of thrombin and markedly prolongs TT.
Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor and therefore prolongs TT.
Dabigatran directly inhibits thrombin, making the thrombin-time assay highly sensitive.

questions.expl: Thrombin time is very sensitive to heparin and direct thrombin inhibition. Warfarin acts on vitamin-K-dependent factor synthesis and usually has little direct effect on thrombin time.

Pure restriction reduces volume/loop size without isolated flattened inspiratory flow.
Fixed obstruction flattens both inspiratory and expiratory loops.

opts.why: Restriction should reduce total lung capacity rather than isolate a low DLCO with preserved volumes.

opts.why: Subdural bleeding is a recognised traction-related complication of CSF hypotension.

opts.why: Orthostatic postdural headache is a direct recognised consequence of a dural leak.
Sixth nerve palsy may develop from traction on the long intracranial abducens nerve.

opts.why: Right middle lobe has medial/lateral divisions, not the characteristic lingular upper/lower pair.
Left lower lobe has superior plus basal segments, not just superior/inferior lingula.
Right lower lobe has superior and multiple basal segments.

Sartorius forms the superficial roof over the adductor canal.

questions.stem: When providing anaesthesia for endovascular treatment of acute ischaemic stroke, the Society of NeuroInterventional Surgery and the Neurocritical Care Society recommend

opts.why: Hyperthermia worsens brain injury rather than improving stroke thrombectomy outcomes.
Severe hyperglycaemia increases ischaemic brain injury risk and should not be permitted.
Deliberate hypotension threatens collateral cerebral perfusion during clot retrieval.

opts.t: Maintain systolic BP approximately 140–180 mmHg during thrombectomy (period guidance)

questions.expl: Periprocedural thrombectomy guidance emphasised avoiding hypotension and targeting an SBP around 140–180 mmHg, with normoxia, normocapnia, normothermia and glucose control.
questions.note: Historical 2020 recommendation; targets after reperfusion vary in later studies/guidelines.

questions.stem: Features indicating an arterial retrobulbar haemorrhage sustained during a peribulbar eyeblock administered for cataract surgery include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Retrobulbar blood can increase ocular pressure above normal.
A fall in visual acuity is a concerning sign of orbital compartment syndrome.
Proptosis reflects expanding retrobulbar volume/pressure.

questions.expl: The recalled EXCEPT choice is chemosis alone, which is nonspecific and commonly occurs after eye blocks. Acute painful proptosis, raised IOP and decreased vision strongly indicate sight-threatening orbital haemorrhage.
questions.note: Chemosis CAN accompany orbital haemorrhage; the exam contrast is specificity, not an absolute impossibility.

questions.stem: A 56 year old patient presents with exertional syncope. The most likely diagnosis is

opts.t: Uncomplicated mitral valve prolapse without obstruction
opts.why: Benign mitral prolapse alone is less characteristic of exertional syncope and dynamic obstruction.
Benign ectopics rarely explain structurally mediated exertional syncope.
Stable primary hypertension does not account for an exertional obstructive syndrome.

questions.expl: Exertional syncope suggests dynamic LV outflow obstruction in HOCM, especially in younger patients, although aortic stenosis and ventricular arrhythmia remain important alternatives.
questions.note: No examination or echo details were supplied; this is the recalled likely diagnosis, not unique from syncope alone.

questions.stem: Your patient underwent a stellate ganglion block 2 hours ago. Prior to discharge you are asked to review the patient in recovery because of a droopy upper eyelid. The patient would also be expected to have ipsilateral

opts.t: Ipsilateral miosis with preserved pupillary light response
Ipsilateral mydriasis with absent light reflex
opts.why: Mydriasis/areflexia would suggest parasympathetic dysfunction or CN III pathology, not successful sympathetic block.
Fixed dilated pupils bilaterally are not the ipsilateral Horner response.
An effective block causes ipsilateral, not exclusively contralateral, miosis.

questions.expl: Stellate block produces Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis and often anhidrosis. Parasympathetic CN III pupillary light reflex remains intact.

questions.stem: The most common cause of airway compromise after anterior cervical spine surgery is

opts.t: Immediate recurrent laryngeal palsy as most common
opts.why: Unilateral vocal-cord palsy causes hoarseness but is not the common acute neck haematoma obstruction mechanism.
Anaphylaxis is possible but not present in every anterior cervical procedure.
Infection generally arises later and is unlikely as the immediate first-hour cause.

questions.expl: Post-anterior cervical-spine surgery, compressive haematoma is a critical early cause of airway compromise. Retropharyngeal oedema is another important cause, often evolving later.
questions.note: Frequency depends on time after surgery; recall emphasises early postoperative haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 100 kg twenty-five year old male presents 2 hours after suffering a 30% Total Body Surface Area electrical burn. He has had no resuscitation fluids. The infusion rate of isotonic crystalloid resuscitation fluid required for this man for the next 6 hours is

opts.why: 500 mL/h delivers only 3 L in six hours, half the calculated initial 6 L requirement.
1,500 mL/h delivers 9 L over six hours, exceeding the Parkland initial half-volume target.
2,000 mL/h gives 12 L within six hours, twice the initial target.

questions.expl: Parkland estimate = 4 mL ×100 kg×30 = 12 L in 24 h, half in the first 8 h from injury (6 L/8 h). At 2 h post injury with no fluids, 6 L must be given over the remaining 6 h = 1,000 mL/h.
questions.note: Parkland is only a starting point; titrate to urine output and perfusion. Electrical burns may require more fluid.

questions.stem: The next patient on your anaesthetist-supported endoscopy list is a fifty-year old woman who has been scheduled for gastroscopy and colonoscopy under sedation, having failed with proceduralist- supervised midazolam and fentanyl sedation in the past. She states that she has egg anaphylaxis, and carries an EpiPen. The most appropriate agent to use for her sedation is

opts.why: Unmonitored fentanyl sedation is inappropriate after failed sedation and may not support safe endoscopy.
General inhalational anaesthesia is not compulsory solely because prior sedation was inadequate.

opts.t: Absolute avoidance of propofol solely due to egg allergy
opts.why: Egg-protein allergy alone does not prohibit modern purified egg-lecithin propofol formulation.

questions.expl: Modern propofol formulations contain purified egg lecithin rather than egg proteins, and egg allergy alone is not a contraindication to propofol.

questions.stem: The most likely cause of hip adduction in a patient undergoing transurethral resection of a bladder tumour is

opts.why: Sciatic nerve does not run near the lateral bladder wall and cannot cause obturator jerk.
Pudendal nerve blockade concerns perineal sensation rather than sudden hip adduction.
Femoral nerve controls knee extension, not adductor spasm.

questions.expl: Electrosurgical current during lateral bladder-wall TURBT can stimulate the obturator nerve and cause sudden adductor contraction ('obturator jerk').

questions.stem: Idarucizumab reverses the anticoagulant effect of

opts.why: Idarucizumab does not bind the Xa inhibitor rivaroxaban.
Warfarin reverses with vitamin K/PCC rather than an anti-dabigatran antibody fragment.
Apixaban is another Xa inhibitor and is not neutralised by idarucizumab.

questions.expl: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that specifically binds dabigatran. Factor Xa inhibitors require different reversal strategies; vitamin K reverses warfarin over time.

questions.stem: During the 21st century, the dominant ozone-depleting substance emitted as a result of medical usage to date has been

opts.why: CO₂ warms the planet but is not an ozone-depleting anaesthetic medical gas as described.
Sevoflurane has greenhouse effects but not N₂O's dominant atmospheric ozone role.
Desflurane has high warming potential but is not the main ozone-depleting medical emission here.

questions.expl: N₂O persists in the atmosphere and contributes to ozone depletion as well as warming. Modern volatile anaesthetics have climate impacts but are not the principal emitted medical ozone-depleting gas.

questions.stem: An analgesic which is a category A drug using the Australian and New Zealand categories for prescribing medicines in pregnancy is

opts.why: Ibuprofen, especially later in pregnancy, carries fetal ductal/renal risks and is not Category A throughout gestation.
Diclofenac in late gestation raises ductus arteriosus/oligohydramnios concerns.

opts.t: Tramadol as a uniformly category-A agent
opts.why: Tramadol does not have the same Category A classification as paracetamol.

questions.expl: Paracetamol is pregnancy category A in Australian classifications and is generally the first-line simple analgesic when indicated.
questions.note: Codeine has also been categorised A in some Australian references; it is deliberately excluded from the reconstructed alternatives to maintain a unique answer.

questions.stem: The ventilator waveforms shown represent

opts.why: A true absent-ventilation tracing would show no repeated supported breaths.
ECG pacemaker spikes are electrical signals, not airway flow/pressure/volume waveforms.

opts.t: Fixed mandatory rate without any patient effort
opts.why: A wholly mandatory untriggered pattern lacks pre-breath inspiratory efforts.

questions.expl: A negative pressure/flow deflection immediately before an assisted breath indicates the patient's inspiratory effort triggers the ventilator. This was the recalled concept.

questions.stem: During spinal surgery, the anaesthetic agent that is least likely to decrease motor evoked potentials is

opts.why: One MAC desflurane strongly reduces motor evoked response amplitude.
High sevoflurane suppresses corticospinal evoked responses.
A large propofol bolus can depress MEP, although carefully titrated TIVA is often preferred.

questions.expl: Ketamine can preserve or augment motor evoked potentials relative to volatile anaesthetics, which dose-dependently depress MEP amplitudes.

questions.stem: A patient has bipolar disorder and is on long term lithium therapy. An analgesic which should be avoided is

opts.t: A small dose of local anaesthetic
opts.why: A local-anaesthetic infiltration dose does not typically inhibit renal lithium clearance.
Paracetamol lacks the key NSAID renal-prostaglandin mechanism.
Nonpharmacological approaches do not increase lithium levels.

questions.expl: NSAIDs can reduce renal lithium clearance, precipitating lithium toxicity; diclofenac is a recognised interacting drug.

questions.stem: In a Blalock–Taussig shunt, blood passes to the pulmonary artery via the

opts.t: Inferior vena cava to pulmonary veins
opts.why: The BT shunt is systemic-artery-to-pulmonary-artery, not IVC-to-pulmonary-vein.
Left atrium is downstream of pulmonary return, not the target of the BT shunt.

opts.t: Subclavian artery through an anastomosis or graft

opts.why: Pulmonary-to-aorta flow is the reverse of the shunt's purpose of increasing pulmonary flow.

questions.expl: Classic BT shunt connects the subclavian artery to a pulmonary artery; modern modified BT shunts commonly use a PTFE conduit.

questions.stem: In the morbidly obese the induction dose of propofol should be calculated based on

opts.why: A universal fixed dose disregards lean mass and physiological variability.

opts.t: Ideal body weight as a universal value for all drugs
opts.why: Ideal body weight for every drug ignores different pharmacokinetics, and propofol bolus usually scales to lean mass.

opts.t: Total body weight for bolus induction without titration
opts.why: Unadjusted total body weight can cause profound induction hypotension from overdose.

questions.expl: Propofol induction dosage in morbid obesity is commonly scaled initially to lean body weight and titrated to effect; total body weight can cause excessive dosing.

questions.stem: A condition that is NOT associated with a raised baseline serum mast cell tryptase level is

opts.t: Alcohol-related liver disease without other explanatory cause

opts.why: Advanced renal failure can reduce tryptase clearance and raise baseline values.
Systemic mastocytosis increases mast-cell mass and baseline tryptase.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia is a recognised genetic cause of elevated baseline tryptase.

questions.expl: Persistently raised basal tryptase may occur with mast-cell disease, hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia and renal dysfunction. Isolated alcohol-related liver disease is not a recognised characteristic cause.
questions.note: Uncommon elevations can occur in other systemic illness; question relies on the recalled option contrast.

questions.stem: The ANZCA Choosing Wisely recommendations advise avoiding all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Unindicated chest imaging in low-risk patients is low-value preoperative investigation.

opts.t: Offering a requested labour epidural to an otherwise low-risk woman
Avoiding unnecessary blood tests based on no clinical indication
opts.why: Unnecessary routine blood tests should be avoided when they won't change management.

opts.why: Unindicated stress tests in asymptomatic low-risk surgery are discouraged.

Glycosuria predisposes to genital/urinary tract infections.

questions.expl: SGLT2 inhibitors increase glucosuria, osmotic diuresis, infections and perioperative euglycaemic DKA risk; hypocalcaemia is not a characteristic primary adverse effect.

questions.stem: A patient with C6 tetraplegia is undergoing removal of bladder stones under general anaesthesia. The blood pressure rises to 166 / 88 mmHg. The appropriate response is to

Intrathecal adrenaline would worsen sympathetic hypertension.

questions.expl: C6 injury predisposes to autonomic dysreflexia from bladder distension/manipulation, provoking severe hypertension. Cease trigger, deepen anaesthesia and treat hypertension if persistent.

Functional independence is scored in the Edmonton Frail Scale.

Clear fluids prohibited for 6 hours in all infants

H₁ blockade is used by antihistamine antiemetics, not NK1 antagonist aprepitant.
5-HT₃ antagonism describes ondansetron-class drugs, not aprepitant.

questions.expl: Aprepitant antagonises NK1 receptors, blocking substance-P-driven emetic signalling, particularly useful in delayed and postoperative emesis.

questions.expl: Wide inspiratory splitting of S₂ occurs when right ventricular outflow obstruction delays pulmonary valve closure, as in pulmonary stenosis.

PRES is uncommon and not the predominant postoperative spine-surgery visual loss pathology.
Corneal abrasion causes pain and surface injury rather than usually severe irreversible blindness.

The disorder commonly fuses digits rather than causing absence of all digits.

ACA infarct is leg-predominant and does not characteristically cause homonymous hemianopia.

questions.expl: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia implicates left occipital cortex/optic radiations, classically left PCA territory; sensory loss can reflect left thalamic involvement.
questions.note: Other lesions can combine deficits; recalled localization favours PCA.

questions.stem: The Brain Trauma Foundation guideline for management of severe head trauma recommend the treatment of intracranial pressures greater than

opts.why: 50 mmHg is far above the guideline intervention threshold and would delay therapy.
5 mmHg is normal/near-normal intracranial pressure and not an indication for hyperosmolar therapy.
10 mmHg is usually within physiologic ranges for an adult.

questions.expl: Brain Trauma Foundation fourth edition recommends treating ICP >22 mmHg as higher values are associated with increased mortality.

questions.stem: The modified Aldrete scoring system is used for determining the

MI diagnosis uses ECG/troponin, not Aldrete domains.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of restless leg syndrome is experiencing significant agitation post op in recovery. After excluding other precipitating causes, the best treatment of the agitation in this patient is

opts.why: Haloperidol D₂ blockade can worsen restless-leg symptoms/akathisia.

opts.t: Droperidol as obligatory first-line in RLS
opts.why: Droperidol also blocks dopamine and may worsen movement symptoms.

opts.t: Midazolam as a cautious short-term sedative after excluding other causes

questions.stem: The most common type of perioperative stroke is

opts.why: Intracerebral haemorrhage is less frequent than ischaemic thromboembolic perioperative stroke.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is a smaller haemorrhagic subtype.

opts.t: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis as the dominant type
opts.why: CVST is not the dominant perioperative stroke mechanism overall.

questions.expl: Most perioperative strokes are ischaemic, frequently embolic, particularly with atrial fibrillation/aortic manipulation; haemorrhagic causes are less common.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a serum sodium of 110mmol/L. A feature NOT consistent with a diagnosis of syndrome of inappropriate antiduretic hormone (SIADH) is

opts.why: Urine sodium >30 is compatible with euvolaemic SIADH when intake is adequate.
Serum hyponatraemia is the presenting abnormality in SIADH.
Urine is generally inappropriately concentrated during SIADH, not maximally dilute.

questions.expl: SIADH causes inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolar plasma; very dilute urine with osmolality <100 suggests suppressed ADH rather than SIADH.

questions.stem: A preeclamptic woman presents with a blood pressure of 150/100 mmHg. An appropriate first line treatment to reduce the blood pressure is

opts.why: Nitroprusside is not mandatory first-line treatment for moderate preeclamptic hypertension and has fetal toxicity concerns.

opts.t: ACE inhibitor started acutely in pregnancy
opts.why: ACE inhibitors can cause fetal renal damage and are avoided in pregnancy.

opts.t: Labetalol (with clinical assessment and local protocol)

questions.expl: Labetalol is a first-line oral/IV agent for hypertension in preeclampsia alongside nifedipine and hydralazine depending on severity and circumstances.
questions.note: BP 150/100 may not require urgent IV reduction; assess persistent values and obstetric protocol.

questions.stem: The approximate maximum flow rate expected with fluid administered (under a pressure bag inflated at 300 mmHg) via an intraosseous needle inserted into the humerus is

opts.why: 5 mL/min is much lower than pressure-assisted humeral IO flow in common studies.
300 mL/min greatly exceeds the standard recalled humeral IO flow estimate.
1 mL/min would indicate nearly absent flow and is not the approximate capacity.

questions.expl: Pressure-assisted humeral intraosseous access can permit flows approximately 60 mL/min, usually faster than tibial IO; actual flow varies with device and pressure.
questions.note: Flow rates are approximate and technique dependent.

questions.stem: You are seeing a 48 year-old woman in your pre-operative clinic for assessment for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. Her co-morbidities include obesity (BMI is 65 kg/m2), hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and polycystic ovary syndrome. Her neck circumference is 38 cm. Her husband states that she snores loudly, but he has never observed her having any apnoeic episodes and she reports no excessive tiredness during the day. Her score using the STOP-BANG questionnaire is

opts.why: One point omits the three documented STOP-BANG risk factors.
Seven requires unreported features such as age>50, male sex, witnessed apnoea, neck circumference etc.
Five also assumes two additional positive risk factors not described.

questions.expl: Scoring: snoring=1, hypertension=1, BMI>35=1; no reported tiredness, witnessed apnoea, age>50, neck>40 or male sex. Total 3.

questions.stem: Infrarenal aortic cross-clamping will alter renal blood flow with a change of

opts.t: About 40% increase in renal blood flow
opts.why: The question concerns reduction of renal blood flow from cross-clamp haemodynamics, not augmentation.
Infrarenal clamping can affect renal flow indirectly despite renal arteries remaining open.

opts.t: About 40% decrease in renal blood flow

opts.why: Renal arteries remain proximal to an infrarenal clamp, so renal flow is reduced but not abolished.

questions.expl: Infrarenal aortic cross-clamping can reduce renal blood flow appreciably (~40%) by neurohumoral and haemodynamic responses, even without direct occlusion of renal arteries.

questions.stem: The coagulopathy that can result from intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is due to

opts.why: Cholestasis does not primarily cause immune platelet destruction.
Intrinsic factor is involved in B12 absorption, not coagulation-factor production.
Congenital factor VIII deficiency does not arise from gestational bile-flow obstruction.

questions.expl: Intrahepatic cholestasis may impair absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K, reducing factors II, VII, IX and X and causing coagulopathy.

questions.stem: A woman with atrial fibrillation has no valvular heart disease. According to AHA guidelines, oral anticoagulants are definitely recommended if her CHA2DS2-VASc score is greater than or equal to

opts.why: Score zero in a woman does not trigger an anticoagulation recommendation.
Female sex alone is not an indication for chronic anticoagulation.

opts.t: Score 2 solely from sex and one other risk factor
opts.why: Two points including sex often warrants individualised assessment rather than unequivocal Class I treatment.

opts.t: CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 3 or more in a woman (historical threshold)

questions.expl: Historical AF guidance strongly recommended oral anticoagulation in women with CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥3 (equivalent to ≥2 non-sex risk factors), with individualized assessment below that threshold.
questions.note: Guideline thresholds and female-sex interpretation have evolved; use contemporary AF recommendations in practice.

questions.stem: A 30 Kg ten-year-old boy has a displaced distal forearm fracture that requires manipulation and plaster. The volume of 0.5% lidocaine that should be used for intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier’s block) is

opts.why: 30 mL at 0.5% supplies 150 mg, 5 mg/kg, exceeding the recalled paediatric dose.
6 mL delivers only 30 mg and insufficient limb vascular spread.
45 mL delivers 225 mg, 7.5 mg/kg, far above the intended IVRA dose.

questions.expl: For Bier block a commonly quoted 0.5% lignocaine dose is 0.6 mL/kg, yielding 18 mL in a 30 kg child (90 mg or 3 mg/kg).
